label: Chess
boundary_note: FIDE's checkmate definition requires attack plus no legal reply; stalemate requires no check. This describes ordinary legal chess endings, not king capture or every possible game termination.

label: Go
boundary_note: The BGA capture explanation uses orthogonal, connected strings and all liberties occupied. The overview does not substitute diagonal adjacency or claim territory is the only scoring system.

label: Shogi
boundary_note: The guide supports Japanese chess and reuse of captured pieces. Drop restrictions and promotion are deliberately omitted because the guide's broader placement claims are unreliable; perpetual check remains a separate rule card.

label: Backgammon
boundary_note: The federation's basic fifteen-checker rules support racing, hits and compulsory bar entry. The description concerns normal movement and does not extend optional scoring conventions to every format.

label: Othello
boundary_note: The official rules require actual outflanking and end play when neither side can move. The card does not require a full board or imply voluntary passing.

label: Contract bridge
boundary_note: The ACBL source specifies partnerships, auction, denomination and dummy. Avoid equating a bid's printed number with total tricks; the overview intentionally omits scoring-format differences.

label: Senet
boundary_note: The museum's funerary association is specifically New Kingdom evidence. The card neither reconstructs uncertain ancient rules as fact nor claims every Egyptian game had a religious function.

label: Twenty Squares
boundary_note: The museum comparison concerns preserved special-square markings on Near Eastern and Egyptian boards. It supports cultural adaptation, not identical rules everywhere or markings on every surviving board.

label: Dick Fosbury
boundary_note: Olympedia provides the 1968 gold and evaluates the technique's influence. The card attributes that interpretation and does not add uninspected biomechanics or imply a long series of later championships.

label: James Naismith
boundary_note: Springfield's historical account explains indoor winter design and reduced roughness. Elevated baskets are a documented design choice, not experimental proof of an injury-prevention effect or all modern rules.

label: En passant
boundary_note: FIDE restricts capture to the immediately following move after the adjacent pawn's two-square initial advance. It remains a legal-move rule, not permission to expose one's own king.

label: Castling
boundary_note: The cited ordinary chess rules distinguish forfeited rights from temporary prevention. Attacks matter on the king's route; the card does not require every rook-transit square to be unattacked.

label: Stalemate
boundary_note: FIDE requires no legal move by the side to move and no check. One trapped piece or an immobile king with other legal moves is insufficient.

label: Dead position in chess
boundary_note: FIDE quantifies over every possible legal sequence, including cooperative play. The card correctly separates absolute mating impossibility from inability to force mate or a likely draw.

label: Touch-move rule
boundary_note: The binding rule applies to the player whose turn it is and the first own piece that can legally move. Revision makes both timing and first-touch ordering explicit.

label: Threefold repetition
boundary_note: FIDE requires a proper claim by the player to move; an intended-move claim precedes execution and includes declaration to the arbiter. Revision adds that procedural boundary while preserving fivefold's automatic contrast.

label: Underpromotion
boundary_note: FIDE permits rook, bishop or knight independently of earlier captures, effective immediately. The card does not claim a particular underpromotion is tactically best or invent a variant's restrictions.

label: Liberties in Go
boundary_note: Only horizontal and vertical neighboring empty points count in the BGA explanation. Connections merge strings for capture; the card does not treat diagonal contact as sufficient.

label: Eyes in Go
boundary_note: Two genuine eyes protect the surrounding group in the cited capture model. The claim is not about superficial holes, false eyes or arbitrary empty points elsewhere on the board.

label: Ko rule
boundary_note: This is the basic immediate-recapture restriction in BGA's introduction. The editorial superko contrast does not claim every longer-cycle rule is satisfied by one intervening play.

label: Seki
boundary_note: BGA's examples support mutual survival through shared liberty constraints. The card intentionally makes no universal claim about whether territory inside seki is scored.

label: Komi
boundary_note: Seven-and-a-half points is explicitly the cited BGA default, not a universal Go constant. Compensation is added to White's score and is distinguished from placing handicap stones.

label: Situational superko
boundary_note: The wording remains tied to the BGA's same-player formulation. Passes and other national variants are not silently folded into a universal repetition definition.

label: Area and territory scoring in Go
boundary_note: The source compares Japanese territory scoring with area systems and AGA pass-stone counting. It does not establish exact identical totals across all rules or handicap arrangements.

label: Doubling cube
boundary_note: The standard cube procedure applies at the start of one's own turn before rolling; some formats temporarily forbid doubling. Revision preserves those limits rather than implying unrestricted offers.

label: Gammon
boundary_note: The multiplier requires the loser to have borne off no checkers; a further bar/home-board condition makes a backgammon. Standard scoring is qualified because the optional Jacoby rule can alter payment.

label: Bearing off in backgammon
boundary_note: All active checkers must be home, and oversized rolls require no higher occupied point. The card does not require bearing off when another legal move is possible.

label: Bar entry in backgammon
boundary_note: The no-entry example loses the turn only when neither die supplies an open entry. The card does not erase legal partial entry or subsequent movement after all barred checkers return.

label: Jacoby rule
boundary_note: The federation labels Jacoby optional and excludes it from standard match play. Revision explicitly preserves that format boundary instead of leaving the optional convention apparently available everywhere.

label: Forced passing in Othello
boundary_note: Passing is forced only without a legal outflank and is forbidden otherwise. A single pass need not end the game; both players lacking moves does, even on an unfilled board.

label: Perpetual check in shogi
boundary_note: The Japanese association's FAQ makes continuous-check repetition a loss on the fourth occurrence. The card stays within that explanation and distinguishes ordinary repetition without asserting an identical rule for chess.

label: Shogi impasse
boundary_note: The professional FAQ requires both kings in enemy territory, no mating prospect and no further captures, with at least twenty-four points each. Revision replaces vague advancement with the specific territorial condition.

label: Duplicate bridge
boundary_note: ACBL supports comparison of the same deals across tables and reduced initial-deal luck. The card says reduces, not eliminates, chance and does not equate all duplicate scoring methods.

label: Vulnerability in bridge
boundary_note: The source separates duplicate board assignment from rubber-game status. The relation now points to contract bridge generally, preserving the subject's coverage of both formats.

label: Dummy in bridge
boundary_note: Exposure occurs after the opening lead, and declarer selects the cards. The information consequence concerns the opponents seeing dummy, not seeing every concealed hand or giving dummy independent strategy choices.

label: Offside in association football
boundary_note: Law 11 judges position at a teammate's play or touch and requires specified active involvement. Revision makes that timing explicit; direct-receipt exceptions remain limited to the three listed restarts.

label: Curveball aerodynamics
boundary_note: NASA's circular arc is an idealized force model that neglects drag-induced changes. The card attributes the approximation and does not describe every real three-dimensional pitch as a circle.

label: Altitude effects on baseball pitches
boundary_note: NASA's lower-density prediction is explicitly all else equal within its simplified model. No measured game outcome or universal magnitude of altitude effect is inferred.

label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
boundary_note: NASA attributes erratic movement to seam-sensitive, time-varying aerodynamic forces. The card preserves that explanatory attribution and does not claim a full quantitative theory or a steady Magnus-only path.

label: Topspin
boundary_note: Cross discusses tennis shots and the combination of racket motion, tilt and incoming spin. Helps and allowing express trajectory potential, not a guarantee that any faster shot lands in bounds.

label: Tennis racket sweet spot
boundary_note: Cross distinguishes a vibration node from other candidate sweet spots. Revision attributes that terminology and states that removing vibration does not cancel rotation or translation forces at the hand.

label: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
boundary_note: The conjugate impact/support point depends on the supported system; adding the hand changes it. The card does not treat the freely suspended center as a universal playing sweet spot.

label: Tennis racket dead spot
boundary_note: Cross's demonstration uses a supported stationary racket and matching effective masses. The card attributes this model and explicitly warns that a moving racket behaves differently.

label: Drafting in cycling
boundary_note: The museum account concerns road-racing wakes and spacing, with a smaller leader benefit. No fixed percentage is generalized to slow mountain biking, every formation or every terrain.

label: Sweeping in curling
boundary_note: The cited source is a 2024 report of athlete practices and disagreements, not a controlled verdict on every technique. Revision makes the date and practitioner-report status explicit.

label: Rhythmic augmentation
boundary_note: The textbook's usual proportional doubling illustrates this rhythmic sense. The card does not equate augmentation with phrase extension or assert every historical use requires an exact factor of two.

label: Musical diminution
boundary_note: The source itself allows exact halving and broader shorter-value usage. Commonly preserves that range rather than falsely requiring a single proportion in every context.

label: Melodic retrograde
boundary_note: The definition concerns reversing note order. The comparison with inversion is editorial and does not assert reversal of every parameter such as articulation, dynamics or performance timing.

label: Melodic inversion
boundary_note: Real and tonal inversion are distinguished in the source. Tonal changes may adjust interval quality to fit the key; the card does not treat all inversion as exact chromatic mirroring.

label: Appoggiatura
boundary_note: The card follows this textbook's non-chord-tone analysis, retaining usual accent and either resolution direction. It does not claim to exhaust historical ornamental meanings of appoggiatura.

label: Pedal point
boundary_note: The source allows bass and upper-voice pedals through changing harmonies. Sustaining a note need not mean literal organ-pedal use or the preparation-resolution pattern of a suspension.

label: Suspension in tonal music
boundary_note: This textbook defines downward stepwise resolution and distinguishes bass suspensions' reference voice. The 4–3 example concerns interval labeling, not absolute pitch or every ornamental usage across music history.

label: Cadential six-four chord
boundary_note: The dominant-function analysis is the cited tonal framework, not a claim about all second-inversion tonic chords. Commonly and the cadential setting preserve that restriction.

label: Additive minimalism
boundary_note: The examples are Glass's particular repetition and duration processes. The card does not define every minimalist work by addition or deny simultaneous subtraction within an additive example.

label: Musical phase shifting
boundary_note: The source expressly distinguishes gradual drift from discrete rotation. Both are retained, so Clapping Music is not inaccurately forced into Piano Phase's continuous speeding procedure.

label: Tonal answer in fugue
boundary_note: The answer is associated with dominant entry but may begin in tonic before moving there. The card preserves that tonal adjustment rather than requiring exact transposition or a dominant starting note.

label: Countersubject
boundary_note: The textbook contrasts recurrent accompaniment with newly composed counterpoint and tracks voices in BWV 847. This does not require every fugue to have a countersubject or keep it in one voice.

label: Pitch (music)
boundary_note: Highness/lowness is perceptual; the octave ratio is restricted to periodic musical tones. The supported missing-fundamental relation avoids confusing perceived pitch with a tuning standard or material pitch.

label: Inharmonicity of musical strings
boundary_note: The stiffness claim concerns real-string resonance modes, with higher modes more affected. Bowing can produce a harmonic operating pattern; the card does not claim every real string has the same inharmonicity.

label: Mode locking in bowed strings
boundary_note: The source discusses periodic stick-slip drive during a steady note. Nearly, can and steady preserve this operating condition rather than asserting every bow stroke or attack is exactly periodic.

label: String harmonic
boundary_note: A light touch selects compatible nodal modes; artificial harmonics additionally stop the string. The violin relation is a performance example, not a claim that all string harmonics are violin-specific.

label: Sympathetic resonance
boundary_note: The cited guitar exercise transfers energy through the bridge into compatible modes. The card does not universalize equal response across all strings or substitute an unsupported purely airborne explanation.

label: Clapping Music
boundary_note: The textbook specifies discrete changes on a downbeat without gradual speeding. The comparison with Piano Phase concerns this timing mechanism, not an exhaustive formal analysis of the composition.

label: Piano Phase
boundary_note: The passage supports a twelve-note pattern and gradual relative acceleration. The card does not assert that the entire work contains only that pattern or prescribe a permanent faster tempo after alignment.

label: Two Pages
boundary_note: The analysis explicitly concerns the opening of the piece. Revision states that boundary and attributes the example to the cited analysis rather than suggesting every section follows the same subtraction pattern.

label: Einstein on the Beach
boundary_note: The claim is restricted to the Train scene's displayed five-chord progression. It does not generalize one minute's additive technique to every scene or the whole opera.

label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
boundary_note: The textbook analyzes this named fugue's exposition and episodes, with subject/countersubject fragments. No uninspected voice count, universal fugue plan or original compositional intention is claimed.

label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
boundary_note: The source labels specific opening-note inversion and an augmented fragment. The card does not claim a complete theme transforms at every recurrence or infer Bach's psychological intention.

label: Adagio for Strings
boundary_note: The source uses a 4–3 analytical label and explains reduction of compound intervals. Revision avoids implying that the sounding interval must literally be a simple fourth in register.

label: Neapolitan chord
boundary_note: The card remains in classical tonal analysis, with first inversion and predominant function described as common. It does not assign that function to every lowered-second sonority in every style.

label: Augmented sixth chord
boundary_note: The source supplies semitone approaches from raised fourth and lowered sixth to dominant pitch classes. Earlier wording was corrected to avoid misleading register convergence; the cited tonal framework stays explicit.

label: Species counterpoint
boundary_note: The source supports rhythmic restrictions and two-to-four-voice teaching examples, not a measured educational outcome. Revision removes an inferred staged-coordination benefit and keeps the described exercises.

label: Counterpoint
boundary_note: The textbook distinguishes simultaneous melodic lines from a homophonic melody-plus-accompaniment texture. The card does not imply harmonic independence, equal salience or effortless tracking by every listener.

label: Missing fundamental
boundary_note: The explanation concerns periodic tones with a harmonic spacing pattern. It does not assert that any arbitrary collection of partials supplies a unique absent fundamental or that physical bass energy is restored.

label: Stretch tuning
boundary_note: Piano stretch responds to stiffness-sharpened partials and beat matching; often and can retain instrument/register variation. No single prescribed stretch or universal nonpiano octave ratio is asserted.

label: Tartini tone
boundary_note: The FAQ permits nonlinear generation in an instrument or auditory system. Can avoids promoting one uncertain physiological mechanism to a universal cause; the frequency-difference example is distinguished from simple resonance transfer.

label: Just intonation
boundary_note: Simple-ratio intervals can conflict across a chain of fifths on fixed-pitch instruments. The card does not call one temperament universally superior or assume all performers can retune every sustained chord.

label: Meantone temperament
boundary_note: The inspected example narrows fifths to improve thirds and has key-dependent limitations. It is a tuning-system subject, with no relation to personality temperament Q80157 or a claim that every meantone variant has pure thirds.

label: Wind-instrument end correction
boundary_note: The effective extra length is an approximation to an open-end reflection. No universal numerical correction is stated, and the comparison to real clarinets remains an editorial qualification of an ideal pipe model.

label: Clarinet overblowing at the twelfth
boundary_note: The odd-mode prediction belongs to a simple cylindrical closed-open model. Near and real-instrument departures explicitly preserve bore, mouthpiece, bell and end-correction limitations.

label: Prepared piano
boundary_note: The Trust documents inserted objects and altered sound. The card avoids claiming a specific material list, universal acoustic effect or that every key is prepared identically.

label: Glass armonica
boundary_note: The FAQ's rubbing-glass account supports frictional excitation and Franklin's rotating bowls. No exact construction dimensions or contested medical/historical effects are added; the bow comparison remains editorial.

The source is the Trust's app interpretation of the composition. The card concerns its three-movement ambient-listening example, not proof of every original score instruction or a promise of current operating-system compatibility.

label: Sonatas and Interludes
boundary_note: The Trust explicitly dates the work and describes supervised sampling with its preparation materials. The card does not invent the cycle's full form, object list or claim to have inspected Cage's score.

label: Gradus ad Parnassum
boundary_note: The textbook identifies Fux's 1725 work and species teaching. Revision removes a potentially misleading longer-note comparison and limits historical interpretation to its documented instructional arrangement.

label: Memory
boundary_note: Encoding, storage and retrieval are functional distinctions in the textbook. The card avoids its stronger computer-storage metaphors, permanent-record language or a claim that exposure alone guarantees retention.

label: Working memory model
boundary_note: This remains an attributed model, including Baddeley's later buffer addition. No anatomical localization, literal files or claim that every component belonged to the original 1974 proposal is made.

label: Sensory memory
boundary_note: The store's placement is explicitly within Atkinson–Shiffrin's model. Brief persistence is distinguished from later retention without turning one sequential model into an undisputed anatomical pathway.

label: Self-reference effect
boundary_note: The textbook describes a relative tendency in remembering personally relevant material. Can avoids an exceptionless benefit or an instructional guarantee for every learner and every kind of content.

label: Procedural memory
boundary_note: The bicycle/driving examples concern skill expressed in performance. The card does not claim all components are unconscious or that inability to verbalize a skill means an absence of learning.

label: Proactive interference
boundary_note: The cited example has older information obstructing newer recall. The card distinguishes retrieval difficulty from erasure and does not infer that every familiar response reflects this mechanism.

label: Retroactive interference
boundary_note: The source gives later learning hindering earlier recall, including email-address examples. The card preserves that direction and avoids interpreting temporary inaccessibility as permanent destruction.

label: Source-monitoring error
boundary_note: Misattribution concerns origin or context rather than necessarily false content. Only the selected Q7565103 is used; no unsupported distinction or merger with the second baseline source-error identity is made.

label: Misinformation effect
boundary_note: The card describes wording effects on reports in Loftus–Palmer studies, using plural studies and can. It does not generalize their samples to all testimony or imply every post-event suggestion changes memory.

label: Henry Molaison
boundary_note: The original paper's abstract verifies the full name; textbook passages support postoperative declarative impairment with retained practiced improvement. No claim of intact all-old-memory or a single perfectly isolated brain lesion is made.

label: Absolute sensory threshold
boundary_note: The fifty-percent criterion is a controlled, probabilistic measurement. The card rejects a sharp never-detected boundary and its editorial SDT comparison distinguishes sensitivity from response criterion.

label: Just-noticeable difference
boundary_note: The source's dark-versus-bright comparison depends on baseline intensity. The card avoids treating Weber scaling as exact across all ranges or confusing difference detection with absolute detection.

label: Sensory adaptation
boundary_note: The selected passage describes reduced conscious notice under continuing stimulation. The card attributes that phenomenological account to OpenStax and avoids asserting one receptor mechanism or equating every distraction with adaptation.

label: Inattentional blindness
boundary_note: The visible unexpected figure is missed during a counting task. The perception parent is directly supported; no universal failure rate, eye defect or unsupported attentional-blink equivalence is asserted.

label: Signal detection theory
boundary_note: The criterion tradeoff presumes the available evidence distribution is held fixed. The card's distinction between sensitivity and willingness to say yes preserves that model logic without importing clinical advice or a specific neural implementation.

label: Figure–ground (perception)
boundary_note: The vase/faces example illustrates reversible segmentation, not a universal order of recognition processes. The card omits the source's contested assumption that figure-ground labeling necessarily precedes all interpretation.

label: Perceptual closure
boundary_note: Fragmented-circle and rectangle examples support a completion tendency. The card does not claim that every incomplete pattern has one compelling whole or that perception literally draws missing pixels.

label: Good continuation
boundary_note: The source says smooth continuous lines are more likely to be perceived. The card keeps tendency language rather than turning a Gestalt heuristic into an exceptionless law.

label: Mental set
boundary_note: The defining problem is persistence after the earlier strategy stops working. The card does not condemn useful routines generally; its fixedness relationship is explicitly a subtype in the text.

label: Functional fixedness
boundary_note: Duncker's box illustrates conventional-use restriction, not a universal inability to repurpose objects. The source's apparent typo about using fixedness to solve the problem is deliberately not propagated.

label: Anchoring effect
boundary_note: The textbook's house-budget example supports disproportionate focus on a focal amount. The card does not invent a measured numerical adjustment effect, universal susceptibility or an experimentally verified intervention.

label: Confirmation bias
boundary_note: The teacher example concerns selective attention to support and neglected counterexamples. This remains one authored control with preserved prior provenance, not two counted meanings because two baseline IDs exist.

label: Hindsight bias
boundary_note: Retrospective confidence is separated from demonstrated foresight. The card does not label every accurate after-the-fact explanation biased or imply that the original outcome was literally unpredictable by anyone.

label: Availability heuristic
boundary_note: Accessible examples can guide judgment even when poorly suited to it. The card does not equate accessibility with falsity or conflate this shortcut with the separately defined representativeness heuristic.

label: Intrinsic motivation
boundary_note: Enjoyment and external reward can coexist, and the baking example is illustrative. Sometimes preserves the source's conflicting findings rather than claiming payment necessarily eliminates enjoyment.

label: Motivation crowding theory
boundary_note: Reward type and expectation condition the cited effects; praise and surprise differ from expected tangible payment. The card avoids a universal crowding-out law and does not add an excluded overjustification identity.

label: Yerkes–Dodson relationship
boundary_note: Task difficulty qualifies any arousal optimum. The card presents a relationship and a possible disruption, not a universal inverted-U law, individual diagnosis or prescriptive stress target.

label: Self-efficacy
boundary_note: The motivational role is attributed to Bandura and concerns perceived capability for a task. The card does not equate self-belief with actual competence, self-esteem or guaranteed persistence.

label: Cognitive dissonance
boundary_note: The smoking example supplies two possible ways to reduce conflict. The card does not endorse discounting evidence or elevate the textbook's disputed self-image restriction into a universal necessary condition.

label: Elaboration likelihood model
boundary_note: The two routes are an explanatory model conditioned on processing motivation and effort. No exhaustive binary, guaranteed durable attitude change or causal superiority of one route is asserted.

label: Foot-in-the-door technique
boundary_note: The result is restricted to the named sign/petition study and a probabilistic increase. It does not promise compliance or portray a small request as sufficient to control later decisions.

label: Asch's conformity experiments
boundary_note: The card retains public line judgments, an unambiguous task and sensitivity to dissent/privacy. Many avoids exporting one historical sample's percentage to all populations or every group setting.

label: Normative social influence
boundary_note: Acceptance-seeking can yield public agreement without private belief. The card does not require every conforming person to be insincere or deny that informational motives can coexist.

label: Informational social influence
boundary_note: The theater-smoke situation is a hypothetical illustration of ambiguity and reliance on others. It is not reported as a specific measured emergency experiment or a guarantee that group information is correct.

label: Milgram's obedience experiments
boundary_note: The learner's shocks were simulated, while participants believed them real; variants changed continuation. The card avoids universal obedience, direct explanation of atrocities or an unqualified population percentage.

label: Psychology
boundary_note: The broad account describes empirical inference from behavior, biology and reports. It neither treats private thoughts as directly visible nor claims every psychological explanation is scientifically established.

label: Inter-rater reliability
boundary_note: Agreement across observers is distinguished from validity. The coding example is an application of the definition, not evidence that agreeing observers are necessarily accurate or free of shared bias.

label: Test–retest reliability
boundary_note: Repeated-administration consistency is the relevant dimension. The card does not demand unchanged scores if the measured trait genuinely changes, and it explicitly avoids equating consistency with validity.

label: Construct validity
boundary_note: The issue is whether the measure captures the intended construct, rather than mere stable scores or apparent plausibility. The card does not reduce validation to one diagnostic statistic.

label: Ecological validity
boundary_note: This is the textbook's real-world-applicability sense, with naturalistic realism traded against control. A realistic setting is not treated as automatically representative of every context or sufficient for causal inference.

label: Experimenter expectancy bias
boundary_note: The source describes interpretation of ambiguous responses when group assignment is known. Helps reduce keeps blinding from being presented as a cure for every measurement error; its inconsistent single-blind aside is not used.

label: Double-blind study
boundary_note: Assignment is concealed from participants and relevant researchers. The card explicitly retains other design requirements and does not imply that the label alone proves successful masking or causation.

label: Research debriefing
boundary_note: The ethics passage specifies purpose, data use and reasons for concealment. The card describes restoring withheld information, not retroactive permission for harmful procedures or a guarantee that explanation eliminates harm.

label: Deception in psychological research
boundary_note: The purpose-concealment rationale is attributed to the cited ethics account and paired with limitations and debriefing. Scientific usefulness is not portrayed as sufficient authorization for any deceptive study.

label: Social desirability bias
boundary_note: Wanting to appear acceptable is one possible source of self-report distortion. The card separates it from misremembering and does not equate every inaccurate answer with deliberate dishonesty.

label: Doctrine of double effect
boundary_note: This is a disputed doctrine with additional proportionality and harm-avoidance requirements. Unintended harm alone is expressly insufficient; the card does not issue a settled moral verdict on any real case.

label: Problem of closeness in double effect
boundary_note: The card presents a criticism about classifying closely connected harms and the influence of moral judgments on descriptions. It does not claim every intention distinction collapses or all side effects are intended.

label: Doing versus allowing harm
boundary_note: Rachels's paired cases test the distinction; the source records objections to their matching and generalization. The card does not conclude that all killing and letting die have identical moral status.

label: Trolley problem
boundary_note: The driver/bystander variants are philosophical tests with disputed verdicts. The card does not turn a stylized case into an agreed practical algorithm or assume one moral distinction settles every variant.

label: Moral luck
boundary_note: The card frames tension between control and ordinary assessment, with outcomes as an example. It asks whether differing blame is justified rather than asserting that luck necessarily excuses or determines responsibility.

label: Problem of temporary intrinsics
boundary_note: The round-to-square plate is a metaphysical problem about property possession at different times. The card does not assert that ordinary change is impossible or endorse one temporal-parts solution.

label: Circumstantial moral luck
boundary_note: Unchosen environments supply different moral tests; they do not force a person's response. The card asks about justified assessment and does not excuse perpetrators solely because their circumstances differed.

label: Constitutive moral luck
boundary_note: Inheritance and upbringing partly shape dispositions. Partly avoids complete determinism, while the card leaves responsibility for character open rather than treating developmental influence as automatic exculpation.

label: Supererogation
boundary_note: Good-but-not-required action is a disputed category. A costly rescue is illustrative, not a necessary cost criterion, and the card acknowledges theories that reject optional moral goodness.

label: Imperfect duty
boundary_note: The stated distinction is explicitly Kantian: latitude in fulfillment does not remove obligation. The card does not impose that account on every tradition or silently equate it with supererogation.

label: Suberogation
boundary_note: Both the mirror category and the ingratitude example are disputed in the source. Proposed and sometimes prevent permissible badness from being presented as an uncontested or easily populated category.

label: Justified true belief analysis
boundary_note: The card calls the tripartite account a proposal and includes the Gettier challenge. It does not state that justified true belief is the accepted sufficient definition of knowledge.

label: Gettier problem
boundary_note: The example is a philosophical counterexample judgment involving justified but accidentally true belief. Some and seem preserve that status; no general claim that every false premise destroys knowledge is added.

label: No-false-lemmas condition
boundary_note: The condition is an attempted repair, explicitly challenged by noninferential cases. The card does not treat absence of false premises as sufficient for knowledge or an accepted consensus analysis.

label: Fake-barn case
boundary_note: Henry's real-barn belief is true and apparently justified in a deceptive environment. The example challenges a knowledge verdict; it is neither an empirical experiment nor proof that all environmental risk defeats knowledge.

label: Epistemic sensitivity
boundary_note: The counterfactual asks whether belief would disappear if the proposition were false. Proposed and disputed retain its philosophical status and prevent conflation with nearby-world safety.

label: Epistemic safety
boundary_note: The account requires truth in nearby worlds where the belief is held, with nearness contested. It is not a settled sufficient test or simple logical contraposition of sensitivity.

label: Epistemic closure
boundary_note: The qualified formulation preserves premise knowledge during competent deduction and actual conclusion belief. It does not imply automatic knowledge of every entailment or resolve the debate about closure.

label: Lottery paradox
boundary_note: The argument assumes a high-probability acceptance rule and unrestricted aggregation. Its conditional opening does not endorse either assumption or equate high probability with knowledge.

label: Preface paradox
boundary_note: The author reasonably believes individual claims while acknowledging likely error across the book. The issue is aggregation of fallible belief, not a contradiction in every single claim or certainty that one named claim is false.

label: Moore's paradox
boundary_note: The difficulty concerns first-person present assertion rather than a logically contradictory proposition. Third-person and past-tense descriptions can be coherent; the card does not collapse assertion norms into truth conditions.

label: Meno's paradox of inquiry
boundary_note: The card states the dilemma and one partial-knowledge response. It neither attributes every modern solution to Plato nor declares inquiry impossible as an established consequence.

label: Epistemology
boundary_note: The broad survey includes varied forms of cognitive success and approaches to evidence. The card does not reduce the field to JTB or endorse one account of knowledge or social influence as settled.

label: Numerical and qualitative identity
boundary_note: One-and-the-same is separated from resemblance and from change through time. The card does not assume the controversial converse that sharing every property necessarily establishes numerical identity.

label: Indiscernibility of identicals
boundary_note: The direction is identity to shared properties, not its converse. The wording concerns referents rather than identical descriptions and does not use opaque belief reports as straightforward property counterexamples.

label: Relative identity
boundary_note: Geach's sortal-relative proposal is explicitly contested. The card distinguishes it from ordinary qualitative similarity and does not present it as a universally accepted replacement for absolute identity.

label: Material constitution
boundary_note: The statue/clay persistence argument is presented as a puzzle among rival interpretations. Seems and the explicit question avoid concluding that two coincident objects necessarily exist.

label: Presentism
boundary_note: Only temporally present objects exist on this view, with timeless abstract objects separately qualified. The card does not say the past never happened or equate present existence with immediate observability.

label: Eternalism
boundary_note: The view includes past and future objects in ontology without locating them in the present. The revised card does not claim past events are currently occurring or that eternalism proves a particular physical theory.

label: Growing block theory
boundary_note: The past-and-present ontology excludes an existing future on this view. It is not equated with eternalism, four-dimensional persistence or an empirically settled model of spacetime.

label: Sorites paradox
boundary_note: The grain chain depends on apparently plausible tolerance steps that generate an unacceptable conclusion. The card does not endorse the universal step premise or claim vagueness already has one agreed solution.

label: Epistemicism about vagueness
boundary_note: Sharp but unknowable boundaries are attributed to this controversial view. The card distinguishes ignorance from semantic gaps and does not state the cutoff has been discovered or measured.

label: Supervaluationism
boundary_note: The standard account evaluates admissible precisifications and preserves excluded middle despite gaps. Many classical laws avoids claiming every enriched logic or variant retains every classical inference.

label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
boundary_note: The distinction is explicitly interpreted differently across Buddhist schools. The card does not impose one metaphysics on all traditions or assert a historically certain origin from a doctrinal attribution.

label: Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream
boundary_note: The modesty lesson is attributed to the cited interpretation. The card does not present literary reversal as proof that waking reality is an illusion or erase alternative readings of the story.

label: Political science
boundary_note: The rules/circumstances/choices framework is an analytical approach to collective decisions involving government. The card does not claim one factor deterministically predicts every political outcome.

label: Constitution (politics)
boundary_note: The textbook distinguishes basic governmental rules from a single codified document. The card does not claim written rights guarantee enforcement or that an uncodified state lacks a constitution.

label: Parliamentary sovereignty
boundary_note: The statement is the UK Parliament's account of legal supremacy and future repeal. Generally and in this account preserve legal and institutional qualifications rather than denying political constraints or all constitutional debate.

label: Uncodified constitution
boundary_note: The UK example contains written statutes despite lacking one consolidated text. The card does not equate uncodified with wholly unwritten, unimportant, unenforceable or unlimited executive discretion.

label: Parliament Act 1911
boundary_note: The legislation concerns most Commons public bills, with specific exclusions. Revision makes the protected extension boundary beyond five years explicit rather than implying every change to parliamentary duration is excluded.

label: Salisbury convention
boundary_note: The convention concerns government manifesto bills and Lords restraint. It is distinguished from a statutory override, without claiming manifesto measures automatically pass every stage or that conventions are identical to law.

label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
boundary_note: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance controls over the simplified overview. Certification, Commons passage, session timing, unamended-passage period, contrary direction and Royal Assent remain distinct requirements; the month does not itself enact the bill.

label: Bicameralism
boundary_note: The two-chamber concept is illustrated by the UK, whose consent exceptions are expressly local. The card does not generalize equal power or Commons-style supremacy to all bicameral legislatures.

label: Mixed-member proportional representation
boundary_note: New Zealand supplies the separate-vote example, and party totals are largely proportional. The card does not promise exact proportionality in every case or universalize its thresholds across MMP jurisdictions.

label: New Zealand MMP threshold
boundary_note: The five-percent-or-electorate-win routes are explicitly New Zealand party rules. The card does not impose them elsewhere or claim an exact list-seat entitlement from threshold eligibility alone.

label: Confidence and supply agreement
boundary_note: The NZ source distinguishes specified support from joining a coalition. The card does not imply identical agreement terms, automatic support for every bill or a universal consequence of proportional representation.

label: Constructive vote of no confidence
boundary_note: Germany's Article 67 requires a majority of all Bundestag members, a successor and a forty-eight-hour interval. No simple majority of votes cast or generic rule for every parliamentary system is substituted.

label: German eternity clause
boundary_note: Article 79 distinguishes inadmissible amendments from those needing two-thirds approval. The examples are nonexhaustive and tied to Germany's Basic Law, not a claim that every constitution has unamendable provisions.

label: Concurrent legislative powers in Germany
boundary_note: The default displacement rule is qualified by Article 72's specified Land departures. The card does not imply unrestricted coexistence or that federal legislation always excludes later state action in every concurrent field.

label: Standing to sue
boundary_note: The cited test is explicitly US federal standing, with actual/imminent concrete injury, causation and likely redressability. It is not offered as every state's rule or a complete treatment of all standing doctrines.

label: Amicus curiae
boundary_note: The definition and procedural sources concern US court practice. Revision makes that setting explicit while retaining court-specific rules rather than an absolute permission requirement or automatic party status.

label: Rule of lenity
boundary_note: The card is explicitly US criminal-law interpretation, not factfinding or all legal ambiguity. Remains ambiguous avoids suggesting every initial uncertainty immediately decides a case for the defendant.

label: Habeas corpus
boundary_note: US federal custody review is distinguished from an ordinary new criminal trial. Procedural limits remain explicit; filing a petition is not represented as guaranteeing a hearing, retrial or release.

label: Stare decisis
boundary_note: The cited account is US law, where horizontal and vertical precedent differ. Revision identifies the Supreme Court's ability to overrule its own precedents rather than suggesting lower courts may disregard binding higher decisions.

label: Burden of proof
boundary_note: US criminal guilt requires proof beyond reasonable doubt; most civil claims use preponderance. Most preserves exceptions, and the card does not give every disputed proposition the same burden or standard.

label: Summary judgment
boundary_note: Rule 56 is explicitly US federal civil procedure. Both no genuine material dispute and entitlement as law are required; the card forbids choosing between genuinely competing evidence merely to avoid trial.

label: Preliminary injunction
boundary_note: The cited Winter/Rule 65 framework is explicitly federal and interim. State rules may differ; likely merits and irreparable harm are not described as an already final judgment for the applicant.

label: Claim preclusion
boundary_note: US litigation is explicit, and generally preserves additional jurisdictional requirements. The bar/merger examples concern the same defendant and cause of action, not every later dispute between the parties.

label: Issue preclusion
boundary_note: The US issue must have been validly, finally and necessarily decided. Can matter preserves further requirements; the card does not promise automatic preclusion against every nonparty or all later claims.

label: Citizens' assemblies
boundary_note: Ireland supplies the procedural example and advisory status. The card does not claim every assembly has binding power, a perfectly representative sample or a proven effect on policy quality.

label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
boundary_note: The source selects from respondents to randomly invited households using demographic strata. Broadly and intended preserve nonresponse and sampling limitations rather than claiming an exact population miniature.

label: Regulatory sandbox
boundary_note: The real-consumer, small-scale, time-limited example is the UK's FCA program. Authorization still applies and national law cannot simply be waived; acceptance is not blanket permission to operate.

label: Freedom of Information Act (United States)
boundary_note: The statute concerns existing federal agency records, not a universal right to all government information. Exemptions remain explicit, and agencies need not create research or new records in response.

label: FOIA segregability
boundary_note: Only reasonably separable nonexempt portions must be released. The card does not assume every partly exempt record contains a useful releasable remainder or that valid exemptions disappear after redaction.

label: Government in the Sunshine Act
boundary_note: Coverage is restricted to defined federal collegial agencies and meetings. Exceptions and formal closure procedures remain explicit; the card does not open every government conversation to observation.

label: Sunset provision
boundary_note: Automatic expiry depends on a specified period and the required renewal process. This describes a legal default, not a guarantee that legislators conduct an effective review or that every program has a sunset.

label: South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
boundary_note: The official historical mandate separates violations, reparations/rehabilitation and amnesty. The card does not claim universal forgiveness, complete reconciliation or successful delivery of every requested remedy.

label: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
boundary_note: The 1997 Khanyile decision supplies a specific nondisclosure refusal. Political context did not guarantee relief, and the card does not imply full disclosure alone was sufficient for amnesty.

label: Brown v. Board of Education
boundary_note: The holding concerns state-imposed racial segregation in public education and equal protection. Later proceedings and resistance are retained; no immediate universal integration or rule for all private conduct is claimed.

label: Gideon v. Wainwright
boundary_note: The named holding is limited here to indigent defendants in state felony trials through constitutional incorporation. It does not promise publicly funded lawyers for all civil cases or every minor criminal proceeding.
